keyQuestions.text: How do the reference repos build bot memory (per-bot and shared) and skills (written, recorded from a demonstration, proposed from use), and how would those map onto Skilled skills and the spec-kit?
How does an OpenBot memory reviewState (unreviewed, confirmed, edited) map onto a skilled-bots needs-you item?
What is the smallest on-disk memory store for a few people on one machine: one JSONL per person plus a per-bot overlay?
How does an OpenBot memory source sync clock (nextSyncAt, syncStatus) map onto our cron and queue triggers?
What does the hermes-muse skills/companion format look like, and is it liftable as a skill store?
How does an OpenBot LearningProposal review (pending_review, approved, rejected with evidence) map onto a Skilled skill proposal?

keyFindings.text: A memory carries a review state of `unreviewed | confirmed | edited`, and an unreviewed memory is never recalled: "a Bot formed it or a source read it in, and no Bot recalls it until the person accepts it." Bot-formed memory therefore arrives inert and needs a human accept before it can influence a run. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:557]

A single-person OpenBot keeps no memory at all: "A single-person OpenBot keeps no memory: every operation here answers not found there." Memory is a team-edition primitive, and the docs confirm "The personal edition does not yet" list Memory. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:10] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:150]

Memory is organization-partitioned and cannot leak across organizations: "What their Bots remember in one organization is never listed or recalled in another they belong to, and a memory named from another organization is answered as not found." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:14]

Memory sources are per-bot app actions with their own sync clock. `MemorySource` requires `botId`, `toolRef` (`appId/toolName`), `args`, `enabled`, `syncStatus` (`idle | running | succeeded | error`), `syncError`, `lastSyncAt` and `nextSyncAt`; `botId` is documented as "The Bot that reads it, and the only one that recalls what it read in." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:640] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:659]

OpenBot's memory is a per-person fact store scoped to an organization, not a per-bot store: the collection path is `/api/v2/organizations/{organizationId}/people/{personId}/memories`, so every fact belongs to a person inside one organization. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:17]

Pausing is a boolean, not a delete: `enabled: false` means "the person has paused it. A paused memory is never recalled." Forgetting is the separate destructive operation. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:554]

Shared versus per-bot memory is one store with two discriminators, not two stores. `formedBy` is `person | import | bot | intelligence`, and `formedByBotId` names the bot that formed the fact; the schema says of that bot "Only that Bot recalls it." A person-formed fact has no `formedByBotId`, so every bot recalls it. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:563] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:570]

Skilled bots has no memory primitive today. The `BOT.md` template's field set is `id`, `trigger`, `runtime`, `budget`, `enabled`, `delivery`, `isolation`, `sandbox`, `secrets`, `precheck`, `spec_folder`, `version` plus a body — no memory field, no store path, no recall hook. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/assets/bot-template.txt:1]

The docs state the same split in one sentence: "Facts you add are shared with all your Bots. Facts a Bot picks up while working stay with that Bot." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:61]

The only occurrence of "memory" in the bots-author skill is the phrase "Start from the shipped template, never from memory", which is about the author's own recall, not a bot memory feature. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/bots-author/SKILL.md:59]

Where CopilotKit Intelligence is present, OpenBot is not the recall engine: Intelligence "holds a copy of each memory the person accepted and does the recall", and OpenBot's own record is the whole store only without it. The smallest-team reading is that OpenBot's memory is a thin record plus a delegated recall service. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:7]

A proposal must be readable before it can be judged: opening a waiting skill "shows its SKILL.md, why it was proposed, and the conversations and recordings it was learned from." The review artifact is the skill file itself plus its evidence, not a diff summary. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/automatic-learning.md:78]

A skill is a named instruction a person runs with `/`, and its record is `slug`, `title`, `summary`, `instructions`, `tools`, `ownerId`, `botIds`, `usableOnYourBots`. The `slug` is both what a person types and the skill's address. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/skills.yaml:294]

A skill's `tools` list is declarative, not a grant: "The actions it needs, as appId/toolName. Naming one gives no Bot access to it: a Bot uses only what it can already use." A skill can therefore be reviewed and approved without widening any bot's reach. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/skills.yaml:314]

Approval is what publishes: `publishedSkillId` is "The skill an approval published. Null until approved." A proposal is therefore a staging record that becomes a skill only on approval, and `operation: remove` means the same pipeline can retire a skill. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/learning.yaml:2167]

Delivery is a per-run snapshot, not a live lookup: shipped remote agents "receive the server-selected, verified skill snapshot for each run". A run's skills are fixed when the run starts. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/automatic-learning.md:107]

Learned guidance never widens capability: "Keep existing tool grants, boundaries, credentials, and manually authored slash skills in place: learned guidance does not grant tools or replace them." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/automatic-learning.md:107]

Sharing is a per-person three-way choice — only their own bots (the default), every bot in the deployment, or the skills they open one by one — and an admin must allow the wider choice first. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/automatic-learning.md:66] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/automatic-learning.md:75]

Skill ownership is three-valued in one record: `ownerId` is a person id, or null when the skill is the organization's; `botIds` is the bots that offer it; `usableOnYourBots` says whether the caller may put it on a bot they own. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/skills.yaml:321] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/skills.yaml:329]

Skill precedence on a run is a fixed three-level order: the bot's own published skills, then the person's own, then any skills another person opened; on a name clash the bot's own wins, then the person's own, and two people's same-named skills are both kept as `<their container>/<name>`. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/automatic-learning.md:65]

Skilled bots has no per-bot skill record. A `BOT.md` has no skills field, so a bot's skills today are whatever the shared skill system discovers, not a list the bot owns. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/assets/bot-template.txt:1]

The "proposed from use" origin is a first-class reviewable object, not a background write. `LearningProposal` carries `runId` (the run that proposed it), `operation` (`add | update | remove`), `status` (`pending_review | approved | rejected`), `title`, `description`, `reason`, `reviewedAt` and `publishedSkillId`. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/learning.yaml:2124] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/learning.yaml:2146]

The sharing index is held in memory and re-read at once on the replica that saved a change and within 30 seconds elsewhere, so no run asks each person's container who shares what. A missing, refusing or slow person container never fails a run. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/automatic-learning.md:66]

The three origins are named explicitly: "A skill is made in one of three ways: you write it, you show the Bot the task once and it records the steps, or OpenBot proposes one from your conversations." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/how-openbot-works.md:68]

Visibility is computed, not stored per viewer: a caller sees their own skills, the ones granted to a team they are in, and the organization's that are granted to no team; an organization's skill granted to teams is listed only to those teams' people, and an admin sees every skill. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/skills.yaml:13]

A full store is compacted, never truncated: merge duplicates or shorten verbose entries in the same batch that saves the new fact, and "Never delete an entry outright; Muse refuses that write". [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/references/memory.md:11]

A model's own output is not memory: "Do not save guesses or summaries Muse produced itself as if the user said them." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/references/memory.md:10]

A patch or remove is pinned to the exact entry it matched, so a concurrent cleanup invalidates the approval rather than silently applying to a different entry. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/references/memory.md:19]

All operational state lives in one SQLite file, `muse/state-v2.db` (WAL), as `entity` rows with an `event` log kept 30 days — one store for goals, notices, receipts and watermarks. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/docs/DESIGN.md:57]

Field types and limits live in exactly one generated file: "All fields, types and limits are in [interface](references/interface.md). That file is generated from the code, so no other page repeats it." This is the cheapest anti-drift device in any of the reference repos. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/SKILL.md:11]

hermes-muse refuses to own a second memory store: "Native memory (or the configured provider) holds what the user said about themselves. Muse does not keep a second user profile, and it never rewrites SOUL, USER or MEMORY." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/references/memory.md:3]

hermes-muse ships exactly one skill, `companion`, and a skill is a directory of markdown: `skills/companion/SKILL.md` (31 lines) plus 21 reference files under `skills/companion/references/`. There is no skill database and no per-skill record. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/SKILL.md:1]

Memory intake is a scheduled job, not a chat-time write: "each hour the job sees new private user messages as short excerpts", and each message is classified `saved` (with `facts`), `context` or `ignored`. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/references/memory.md:6]

Secrets are excluded by construction rather than by policy: "Never save secrets: excerpts are redacted, so keep them that way." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/references/memory.md:9]

Staged writes are approved from the CLI, not a web page: `/memory approve <id>`, `/memory reject <id>` and `/memory pending` list and resolve them. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/references/memory.md:17]

The classification is a required enum on the job's submit payload, so a run cannot finish without deciding what each message was: `disposition` is required and is `saved / ignored / context`. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/references/interface.md:242]

The compaction rule is enforced in code, not prose: a `pre_tool_call` hook "refuses a native `memory` call with more removes than patches, and every change is recorded by code. Muse never writes the memory files itself." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/docs/DESIGN.md:123]
The licence is MIT, so the skill directory and the memory reference are liftable with attribution. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/LICENSE:1]

The skill body is a router, not a procedure: it names the two tools (`muse_manage` for the user's conversation, `muse_job` for its own runs) and then points at reference files by topic. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/SKILL.md:7]

The SKILL.md frontmatter is only `name`, `description` and `version`. There is no tools list, no owner, no bot list and no review state — the fields OpenBot's `Skill` record carries are simply absent. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/SKILL.md:1]

The upkeep job is `memory-upkeep`, hourly and local, and a store at least 90% full is named in the packet as `memory_full` (at most 3 per packet). [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/docs/DESIGN.md:134] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/docs/DESIGN.md:163]

A skill is invoked by typing `/name` in a message, and its instructions reach the model wrapped in `<skill_content name="...">`, which is also how a chat summary finds them again. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/skills.js:13]

Compaction is a model rewrite, not a delete: `tidy` asks a model to write the memory anew as one whole, merging duplicates and keeping only the later of two disagreeing records. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/memory.js:12]

Each record is `{id, text, at, by}` where `by` is `'agent'` or `'user'`. Provenance is a two-value field, not a review state: an agent-written record is live immediately and the user edits or removes it in Settings. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/memory.js:87]

Extraction is a separate model call after each reply, and the stated reason is that the working model cannot be trusted to do it: "Models of every size let facts pass by while they work, the weaker ones nearly all of them". [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/fact-keeper.js:4]

OpenGhost keeps one shared memory of the user as a flat list of short records with hard limits: 400 characters per record, 60 records, and "crowded" at 28 records or 3600 characters total. The whole design fits in one constant. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/memory.js:11]

OpenGhost splits per-chat from shared in exactly the way the node asks about: the chat's "record" is a private file per chat that outlives its summaries, and the "memory" is shared by all the user's chats. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/fact-keeper.js:4]

OpenGhost's skills are the open Agent Skills format (agentskills.io): a folder with a `SKILL.md`, a YAML head with name and description, then instructions, with `scripts/`, `references/` and `assets/` read only when the instructions point at them. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/desktop/skills.js:3]

openhuman-main is the opposite end: a full memory subsystem, not a store. It binds a vendored TinyMemory engine with turn hooks (pre-turn pack, post-turn log, compaction recall), a background job queue, a shared "brain" of documents by source type, a `[[memory.sources]]` registry (folder, file, link, github, rss, composio), consent-gated backfill and import, and one `memory` agent tool. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-core/src/memory/mod.rs:1]

openhuman's memory tool is budgeted and fails open: a refusal carries `openhuman.memory_budget` metadata and the run continues with "Continue answering the user's request without memory. Do not retry memory in this run." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-core/src/memory/tools.rs:24]

openhuman's per-agent split is configuration, not schema: `identity_pins` maps each agent id to `{agent_id, root, recall}`, so a bot gets its own memory root and its own recall switch. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-core/src/memory/scope.rs:13]

Skill discovery reuses other agents' folders rather than inventing one: `~/.agents/skills`, `~/.claude/skills`, and the same two inside the project, with the project's own winning over the user's of the same name; new skills are written to `~/.agents/skills`. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/desktop/skills.js:9]

The extractor is told to write a changed fact as an edit so "no two lines ever disagree", and to prefer the per-chat record when unsure: "a line too many costs little, a lost fact costs much." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/fact-keeper.js:40]

The licence split decides what is liftable: OpenBot, OpenGhost and hermes-muse are MIT; openhuman is GPL-3.0; OpenMausBot, rakazo, turnstone and buzz are Apache-2.0. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/LICENSE:1] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/LICENSE:1] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/LICENSE:1] [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/LICENSE:1]

The tidy result is accepted only on four conditions: non-empty, strictly shorter than what it replaced, memory still switched on, and every source record still present. Records added or changed meanwhile survive untouched. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/memory.js:145]

All four repos converge on one memory store with a scope discriminator, not two stores. OpenBot uses `formedBy` plus `formedByBotId`; openhuman maps each agent to `{agent_id, root, recall}`; OpenGhost keeps one shared memory beside a per-chat record; hermes-muse delegates entirely to the host. No repo keeps a separate "shared memory" and "bot memory" database. [INFERENCE: based on specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:563, specs/system-skilled-bots/context/openhuman-main/crates/openhuman-core/src/memory/scope.rs:13, specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/fact-keeper.js:4, specs/system-skilled-bots/context/hermes-muse-main/skills/companion/references/memory.md:3]

OpenBot's `reviewState` gate is the one behaviour worth copying even at small-team size, because it is exactly what stops a bot's own guess from becoming a fact every other bot recalls. OpenGhost's live-write posture is defensible only because it is single-user; a shared host with several people needs the gate. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:557]

Skilled already has the skill half. Sixteen skills are discovered automatically from a valid `SKILL.md` frontmatter plus `graph-metadata.json`, and "no manual registration step exists". [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/README.txt:33]

Skilled's `SKILL.md` frontmatter is already richer than hermes-muse's three fields and close to OpenBot's `Skill` record: `name`, `description`, `allowed-tools`, `version`, `trigger_phrases`, `keywords`, `intent_signals`. What it lacks is `ownerId`, `botIds` and a review state. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skill-advisor/SKILL.md:1]

The "proposed from use" origin maps onto two things Skilled already has: a proposal is a candidate `SKILL.md` written into a proposals folder, and its approval is a needs-you item. That reuses the existing skill discovery and the existing approval surface instead of adding a review UI. [INFERENCE: based on specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/learning.yaml:2124 and the needs-you item surface in .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/]

The "recorded from a demonstration" origin has no Skilled equivalent and no cheap one. OpenBot delegates it to an external Learning service with recordings, per-person containers and a review queue; the recording path alone needs a browser recorder and a container per person. The smallest honest answer is to skip it and say so. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/docs/automatic-learning.md:62]

The "written" origin already works with no change: a person writes a `SKILL.md`, the frontmatter and graph metadata make it discoverable, and the advisor routes to it. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/README.txt:33]

The licence position is clean for the two files worth lifting: OpenGhost's `memory.js` and `desktop/skills.js` are MIT, so both can be ported with attribution. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/LICENSE:1]

The mapping is therefore asymmetric and small: skills need one new frontmatter field (`bots`) and one new folder (`proposals/`); memory needs one new file per scope and one new command to read and write it. Neither needs a service, a database, a container or a review UI. [INFERENCE: based on findings 3-8]

The smallest workable shape is OpenGhost's: one shared memory file of short records plus a per-chat record file, each record `{id, text, at, by}`, with four hard limits in one constant. It is 213 lines and needs no service, no database and no admin. [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenGhost-main/memory.js:11]

The spec-kit already owns the per-person continuity surface: `handover.md`, then the `_memory.continuity` frontmatter block, written by `generate-context.js` through `/speckit:save`. That is the natural home for a person's shared memory rather than a new store. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/SKILL.md:138]

`bots answer <item-id> <text>` checks the answer for secret literals first, because it reaches the resumed run's prompt, then writes it on the item and enqueues one `resume` request keyed by the item id. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/feature-catalog/operator-loop/needs-you-answer.md:22]

A needs-you item is written by the runner, not by the model: the prompt tells the child to print a `[NEEDS-DECISION] ` line with its question and optional `[OPTION] ` lines, and the runner writes one item and ends the run as `awaiting-decision` with exit 5. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/feature-catalog/operator-loop/needs-you-items.md:24]

An item expires after the repository's needs-you expiry, seven days by default, and an expired item is listed as expired without being rewritten. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/feature-catalog/operator-loop/needs-you-items.md:26]

An open item holds every later run of its bot, refused before dispatch, and the hold lifts once the item is answered or expires. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/feature-catalog/operator-loop/needs-you-items.md:28]

Item state is `open | answered | expired` and is "derived from its fields every time it is read and never stored, so it can never disagree with them." [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/needs-you.ts:49]

OpenBot's three-value `reviewState` collapses to two here: `unreviewed` is the item's open state and `confirmed` is the answered state. `edited` is not a third state — it is what the answer text carries when the person rewrites the fact before confirming. [INFERENCE: based on specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:557 and .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/feature-catalog/operator-loop/needs-you-answer.md:22]

The item already carries `evidence: string[]`, which is the same field OpenBot's proposal review needs: "the conversations and recordings it was learned from". [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/needs-you.ts:41]

The item shape is `{id, runId, botId, identity, question, options, createdAt, expiresAt, evidence, prompt, specFolder, answer, resumeRequestId}`, and `id` is documented as "The parked run's id, so one run writes at most one item." [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/needs-you.ts:29]

The mapping is partial, not direct: a memory review is not run-scoped, but a needs-you item's `id` is the parked run's id and an open item holds the bot. Reusing the item unchanged would hold a bot on every unreviewed fact, which is the opposite of what a memory gate should do. [INFERENCE: based on .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/needs-you.ts:29 and .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/feature-catalog/operator-loop/needs-you-items.md:28]

The resumed run's prompt is the parked run's own prompt, then the question, any offered options and the answer, with an instruction to continue from where that run stopped; it binds the same spec folder and reopens the kept worktree. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/feature-catalog/operator-loop/needs-you-answer.md:26]

The smallest correct mapping is a review item with the same file shape and the same derived state but no hold and no resume: `id` becomes the memory fact id, `prompt` / `specFolder` / `resumeRequestId` drop out, and `answer` becomes `confirmed | rejected`. That keeps one operator surface (`bots inbox`) and one answer verb. [INFERENCE: based on findings 2, 3 and 9]

A single-person install should keep no memory file at all, matching OpenBot: the person file is created on the first fact a bot forms, so an install with one person and no review never grows a memory folder. [INFERENCE: based on findings 9 and 13]
Every state folder is created owner-only with mode `0o700`, the same rule the env-secret guard applies to its own state. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/state-root.ts:161]

JSONL is the wrong format for this store: `writeStateAtomic` already does a whole-file temp write, fsync and rename, and `writeStateIfChangedAtomic` skips an unchanged write, so a JSON array per person gets atomicity for free, while JSONL would need a new append-and-fsync path and a line-level parser. [INFERENCE: based on .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/runtime/lib/deep-loop/atomic-state.ts:413]

One JSON file per thing is the existing convention: `recordFile` is `{records}/{runId}.json` and `needsYouFile` is `{needsYou}/{itemId}.json`, both guarded by `isSafeSegment` so an id cannot escape its folder or hide as a dot file. [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/state-root.ts:176] [SOURCE: .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/lib/state-root.ts:181]

OpenBot keeps no memory at all for a single-person deployment: "A single-person OpenBot keeps no memory: every operation here answers not found there." [SOURCE: specs/system-skilled-bots/context/OpenBot-main/api/openapi/memory.yaml:10]

The reuse inventory, with repo, path and licence: OpenBot's four-part routine sentence (`docs/routines.md:16`, MIT), OpenBot's approvals precedence ladder (`docs/approvals.md:3`, MIT), OpenBot's derived review state and idempotent approve (`api/openapi/learning.yaml:1130`, MIT), OpenGhost's bounded memory with a tidy rewrite (`memory.js:11`, MIT), and hermes-muse's staged-write pinning rule (`skills/companion/references/memory.md:20`, MIT). [INFERENCE: based on findings 6 through 10]

The skip list, with a reason each: Kubernetes (release promotion for a cluster a small team does not run), managed upgrades (a vendor agent tied to that chart), multi-tenant (memory scoped per organization when a small team is one organization), enterprise roles (an `admin` tier that governs sign-in when there is no sign-in), mobile (632 files for a client that cannot run a launchd job), and PostgreSQL plus Compose (a database server and a container supervisor where the runtime is a Node CLI with a SQLite index). [INFERENCE: based on findings 1 through 5 and iteration 12]
The terminal client comes last because it draws the four surfaces the earlier items create, and building it first would mean drawing empty screens. [INFERENCE: based on iteration 11 and finding 15]
The whole build is seven items, none of which needs a new service, a database server, a container or a sign-in. [INFERENCE: based on findings 12, 15 and 16]

ruledOutDirections.text: Reading the generated TypeScript client under `app/src/lib/api/generated/memory/` as the model source. It is generated from `api/openapi/memory.yaml`, so the spec is the authority and the client adds no semantics.

Searching for a memory implementation directory under `api/` returned only `api/openapi/memory.yaml`. OpenBot's memory server code is not in this reference checkout, so the model must be read from the spec and docs. This bounds how far "how it is built" can be answered for memory: the contract is available, the implementation is not.

Treating `formedBy: intelligence` as a fourth memory scope. It is a provenance value for a fact the backend holds that OpenBot formed no record of, and the schema says such a fact "can be edited or forgotten but not paused" — a storage-origin distinction, not a scope.
Modelling the three origins as three storage locations. All three produce the same `Skill` record; only the proposal path adds a staging row, so the origin is provenance rather than a separate store.

Searching `skills.yaml` for a "taught" or "recorded" origin field returned nothing. The recorded-from-a-demonstration origin is not a field on `Skill`; it is a Learning path that ends in the same record. Any design that adds an `origin` column to a skill store is inventing a distinction OpenBot does not persist.

Treating `tools` on a skill as a capability grant. The schema says naming an action gives no bot access to it, so a skill cannot be used to escalate a bot's reach and does not need a grant check at approval time.
Building a second memory store beside the host's. hermes-muse explicitly declines to, and the reason is structural: two stores drift and the model cannot tell which is authoritative.

Copying hermes-muse's `SKILL.md` frontmatter as a skill record. It carries three fields and no scoping, so it cannot express who may use a skill or which bot offers it; the OpenBot `Skill` record is the better shape and the Skilled `SKILL.md` frontmatter is already richer.

Looking for a skill-proposal or skill-review path in hermes-muse. There is none: its one skill is hand-authored and shipped, so it offers no evidence for the "proposed from use" origin. That origin has to be answered from OpenBot and from Skilled's own spec-kit, not from this repo.
Copying openhuman's memory subsystem. It is a vendored engine with a job queue, a document brain and a source registry, and it is GPL-3.0. For a small team it is the wrong size and the wrong licence.

Looking for a skill-proposal path in OpenGhost. Its skills are discovered from folders and installed from a link; there is no proposal queue. The "proposed from use" origin remains an OpenBot-only pattern in this repo set.

Treating OpenGhost's `by` field as a review gate. An agent-written record is live at once; the user's control is edit and remove, not approve. That is a different trust posture from OpenBot's `reviewState` and the difference matters for the recommendation.
A separate shared-memory store and per-bot memory store. No reference repo does it, and it doubles the write path for no gain.
Building the "recorded from a demonstration" origin. It needs a recorder, a container per person and an external analysis service, which is the enterprise shape D3 puts on the skip list.
Copying OpenBot's `reviewState` as a three-value enum with an `edited` state. Two values (`unreviewed`, `confirmed`) carry the gate; `edited` is a UI affordance, not a recall rule.

Searching Skilled for an existing memory store to extend. There is none: the only continuity surface is the spec-kit's per-packet `handover.md` and `_memory.continuity`, which is per-packet, not per-person or per-bot. The gap is real and cannot be closed by configuration.

A separate review UI. `bots inbox` already lists open items and `bots answer` already resolves them; a second surface would be the "two pages answering the same question" that OpenBot's own rules forbid.
Adding a third `edited` review state. The answer text already carries the rewrite, so a third state would need its own transition rules for no recall benefit.

Looking for a non-holding item class in `needs-you.ts`. There is none: `holdForBot` returns a hold for any open item of the bot, so a non-holding review item is a new shape rather than a configuration of the existing one.
Reusing `NeedsYouItem` verbatim for memory review. Its `id` is the run id and its open state holds the bot, so a single unreviewed fact would stop every later run of that bot.

A second SQLite database for memory. The index is SQLite because it answers cross-identity queries; memory is read whole by one bot at a time, so a database would add a schema and a migration for no query benefit.
Keying memory by repository identity only. That is what the runtime does today, and it makes a person's facts vanish when they move to another checkout.
Looking for an existing per-person key to hang memory on. There is none: `identityKey` is derived from `owner/name`, and no other identity dimension exists in the runtime.
One JSON file per fact, matching `records/` and `needs-you/`. A memory of a few hundred facts would become a few hundred files, and recall would read the whole folder on every run.
One JSONL per person. The runtime's atomic write helper is whole-file, so JSONL buys nothing and costs a new append path plus a line-level parser.
A fifth trigger kind for memory sync. The four kinds already cover a timed read-in, and a new kind would need its own validation, install path and drift rule.
A separate sync scheduler beside the drain job. The drain job already runs on a throttle with backoff and already claims requests from the inbox.
Looking for a next-fire calculator in the runtime. There is none by design: `NEXT_FIRE_UNKNOWN` is the only value the installer ever reports for `nextFire`.
Storing `nextSyncAt` as a computed timestamp. The runtime deliberately reports `UNKNOWN` for a next fire because no launchd surface reports one, so a stored value would be a guess that goes stale.
Storing `syncStatus` as a field. Every one of its four values is already readable from the queue and the last run record, so a stored copy could disagree with them.

A database-backed skill store. hermes-muse keeps skills as markdown and state in SQLite, and the skill is explicitly forbidden to hand-edit that database; a skill store in a database would invert that split.
A new frontmatter schema. Skilled's five keys already cover what the companion's three do, and adding a key would need a discovery-rule change for no gain.
A separate proposal UI. hermes-muse reviews a staged write with a slash command and an id, which is the same shape as `bots inbox` plus `bots answer`.

Lifting the companion folder as a template. Its 21 references are all Muse domain pages (goals, dispatch, proactivity, sources, calendar, weather, feed, briefings), so copying the folder would import a domain, not a format.
Searching hermes-muse for a skill-proposal or skill-creation mechanism. There is none: the companion skill is authored, never generated, and the only staged-write path is for memory.
A new review command beside `bots answer`. The needs-you item already carries a question, options, an answer and evidence, which is the whole proposal review.
Applying a proposal without the skill-advisor's trusted mutation path. That path is the only write the advisor trusts, and a second write path would bypass its gate.
Embedding evidence in the proposal. OpenBot serves evidence from its own endpoint so a reviewer reads it on demand; embedding it would make every proposal carry its whole transcript.
Looking for an existing proposal or draft mechanism in `.skilled/skills/`. There is none: skills are authored directly, and the only staged-write pattern in the tree is the needs-you item.

Storing `status` as a field on the proposal. Every value is readable from the answer and the applied skill, so a stored copy could disagree with them, which is the same failure the needs-you item avoids.
A web UI served from the CLI. The TUI needs no HTTP server or sidecar, and a served UI would add a port, a session and a browser to a tool that already runs in the terminal.
Building a Tauri shell first. OpenBot's native side exists to install and supervise Compose, and a runtime that boots in-process has nothing to install or supervise.
Copying openhuman's four tabs as-is. Logs, Chat, Config and Settings are its own split; the OpenBot surfaces are conversations, approvals, activity and routines.
Searching the other seven repos for a terminal UI. Only openhuman ships one; OpenBot, buzz and openhuman's own app are Tauri, and OpenGhost and hermes-muse are desktop shells.
Treating the terminal as a reduced client. openhuman's TUI drives the same `web_chat` surface as its desktop app, so the surface is shared rather than reimplemented.
A session token or cookie. The state root's owner and mode already decide who can read and write, and a token would be a second authority that can disagree with the filesystem.
Building sign-in. OpenBot's own single-person install has none, and a few people on one machine already have an OS identity that a session would only duplicate.
Looking for a role or permission check anywhere in the runtime. There is none: `bots answer` writes the answer after a secret check and nothing else.
Per-bot memory ownership. OpenBot scopes memory to the person and the organization, and a per-bot store would make a person's facts disappear when the bot is renamed.
Three roles. `admin` governs people, sign-in and policy; with no sign-in there is nothing for it to govern, so it collapses into `owner`.
Building the terminal client first. It would draw four empty surfaces until the memory, review, proposal and routine items exist.
Keeping the multi-tenant memory scope. A small team is one organization, so the second scope would be a branch nothing takes.
Lifting OpenBot's desktop shell. Its native side installs and supervises Compose, which this runtime does not have.
Lifting openhuman's TUI code. GPL-3.0 cannot be relicensed into this tree, so only the shape transfers.
Looking for a permissively licensed terminal client to lift. The only one in the set is openhuman's, and it is GPL-3.0.
